2.7 Phylodynamic Characterization of OROV 𝑀 1 𝐿 2 𝑆 2 Genotype in Brazil

When the DL estimators were applied to the three retained clusters, the inferred epidemiological parameters were broadly comparable (overlapping PIs) despite differences in cluster size, temporal dynamics, and outbreak setting (Fig. 3b). Median estimates of the vector-to-human reproduction number, 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 , were greater than 1 in all three clusters, ranging from 1.09 in CE-2024 to 1.45 in AM-I, with an intermediate value of 1.38 in ES-I. Greater variation was observed for the human-to-vector reproduction number, 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 , with median estimates of 0.73 in AM-I, 0.85 in ES-I, and 1.55 in CE-2024. Despite these differences in the directional components of transmission, the composite human-to-human reproduction number, 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 , had median estimates greater than 1 in all three clusters, with the highest value inferred for CE-2024 (1.81), followed by AM-I (1.32) and ES-I (1.15). The duration-related parameters showed comparatively limited variation among clusters. Median estimates of the total duration of infection in vectors, 𝐷 𝑉 , ranged from 15.4 days in AM-I to 18.5 days in ES-I, with an intermediate value of 17.3 days in CE-2024. Likewise, median estimates of the total duration of infection in humans, 𝐷 𝐻 , ranged from 9.42 days in AM-I to 12.3 days in CE-2024, with an estimate of 10.8 days in ES-I. The inferred vector-to-human ratio, 𝑉/𝐻, was also similar across clusters, with median estimates of 1.32 in AM-I, 1.52 in CE-2024, and 1.47 in ES-I.

We also assessed the sensitivity of 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 inference to uncertainty in the genomic sampling proportion. Because OROV infections are likely under-ascertained, the true number of cases may exceed those reported through routine surveillance, resulting in a lower genomic sampling proportion than initially estimated. Accordingly, inference was repeated for each of the three genomic clusters after cumulatively increasing the estimated number of cases in 10% increments, up to 50% above the baseline estimate, thereby progressively reducing the assumed genomic sampling proportion (Fig. 3c). Across all three clusters, 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 estimates were only modestly affected. Median 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 decreased from 1.32 to 1.26 in AM-I (∼ 4.5%) and from 1.81 to 1.76 in CE-2024 (∼ 2.5%), whereas virtually no change was observed for ES-I (1.154 to 1.155).

2.8 Temporal Dynamics of 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 Across OROV Genomic Clusters

To further characterize the temporal dynamics of 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 across the three genomic clusters retained for analysis, cumulative 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 estimates were obtained by progressively slicing each phylogenetic tree and incorporating increasing amounts of information from its root toward the most recently sampled sequence (Fig. 3d-f). Starting from the inferred 𝑡 MRCA , each tree was truncated at successive seven-day intervals, and 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 was re-estimated using all phylogenetic information available up to each time point. Inference was initiated once the truncated tree contained at least 30 tips, corresponding to the minimum tree size represented in the datasets used to train the DL estimators. Whereas whole-cluster analyses yielded broadly comparable 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 estimates, this cumulative approach enabled transmission dynamics to be examined in relation to the temporal accumulation of genomic information and the epidemiological context of each cluster, including the timing of genomic sampling, reported case incidence, and seasonal patterns.

AM-I (Fig. 3d and Table 2) was the largest of the three clusters (n = 260 genomes) and was inferred to have originated in Amazonas state in mid-2023 (𝑡 MRCA = 20 August 2023). Genomes assigned to this cluster were sampled from late November 2023 to late February 2024 (∼ 3 months), a period that largely coincided with the rainy season in the state. AM-I accounted for more than 80% of the genomes sampled in Amazonas during this interval and comprised predominantly sequences obtained in the state capital, Manaus (∼ 70%). The concentration of genomic sampling early in the outbreak, with more than 50% of sequences collected by the end of December 2023, provided sufficient phylogenetic information to estimate cumulative 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 during the phase of case expansion in the state. Cumulative inference indicated that 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 peaked above 4.0 in late December 2023 (4.4, 95% PI: 2.6-5.4), approximately three weeks before reported case counts in Amazonas reached their peak of approximately 350 cases per epidemiological week (EW), after which 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 progressively declined until its final value of 1.3 (95% PI: 0.9-2.0).

CE-2024 (n = 90 genomes, Fig. 3e and Table 2) represented a subcluster within the broader CE cluster, which comprised all genomes sampled in Ceará. This subcluster was inferred to have originated in mid-May 2024 (𝑡 MRCA = 17 April 2024), during the rainy season in the state. Nevertheless, the vast majority (> 95%) of CE-2024 genomes were sampled subsequently, between June and August 2024. Spatially, all genomes assigned to this subcluster were obtained from municipalities within the Maciço de Baturité, a humid montane enclave embedded in the semiarid region of Ceará and characterized by remnants of tropical humid forest. Reported cases in the state followed a broadly concordant temporal pattern, increasing progressively to a peak of nearly 40 cases per EW in mid-August before declining throughout September. More than 75% of CE-2024 genomes were sampled between mid-July and August 2024, such that sufficient phylogenetic information for cumulative inference became available only from late July onward, when reported case counts were already approaching their peak. At the earliest time point for which cumulative inference was possible, the median 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 was estimated at 3.0 (95% PI: 1.5-4.5) and subsequently declined as the local outbreak progressed until reaching 1.8 (95% PI: 1.2-3.0).

ES-I (Fig. 3f and Table 2) was inferred to have originated in late March 2024 (𝑡 MRCA = 24 March 2024) and exhibited a markedly prolonged pattern of circulation, with genomes sampled across more than 40 municipalities before, during, and after the 2025 rainy season in the state. ES-I was the largest (n = 124 genomes) of the four genomic clusters identified in the state, substantially exceeding the sizes of the other three clusters (𝑛 = 6, 9, and 60) and accounting for approximately 60% of all genomes sampled in Espírito Santo. Distinct from the genomic sampling, reported cases in the state over the same period were strongly concentrated during the 2025 rainy season. Although sufficient phylogenetic information to support cumulative 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 inference became available during the rise in reported case counts, ES-I had already been detected through genomic surveillance in the state for more than six months by that time. The median cumulative 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 fluctuated only modestly, from approximately 1.0 (95% PI: 0.4-2.1) in early January to 1.2 (95% PI: 0.5-1.8) in early April, remaining relatively stable throughout the period for which inference was possible.

3 Discussion

Here, we introduce the Birth-Death Exposed-Infectious Vector-Human (BDEIVH) model, a novel phylodynamic framework that explicitly represents the alternating human-vector transmission cycle characteristic of arboviruses, and apply it to investigate the expansion of the OROV 𝑀 1 𝐿 2 𝑆 2 lineage in Brazil. The model incorporates the directional reproduction numbers 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 and 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 and their product, 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 , defined as the expected number of secondary human infections generated by a single infectious human through one complete vector-mediated transmission cycle. It also describes the total durations of infection in humans (𝐷 𝐻 ) and vectors (𝐷 𝑉 ) and the ratio of infected vectors to infected humans (𝑉/𝐻). Implemented within a neural-network framework adapted from PhyloCNN [68], the BDEIVH estimator recovered key epidemiological parameters with low bias, although precision varied across parameters and tree sizes, overall improving with tree size. Performance was largely maintained when simulated trees were modified to approximate the limited phylogenetic resolution of empirical OROV data. Notably, 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 estimates were substantially more accurate than those obtained using simpler birth-death formulations applied to the same trees, illustrating how biologically informed model complexity can improve phylodynamic inference. Application to major transmission clusters in Brazil supported sustained transmission both in historically endemic regions and in areas where autochthonous OROV transmission had not been documented before the 2022-2025 outbreak.

The principal limitation of this study was the scarcity of empirical data to inform the biological assumptions underlying our simulation-based inference. In particular, limited knowledge of the extrinsic incubation period and lifespan of C. paraensis, presumed to be the main vector during the outbreak, prevented us from specifying separate, empirically informed ranges for the incubation and infectious periods in vectors. A further constraint was the absence of genomic sequences from infected vectors. Obtaining such data remains challenging, given reported detection frequencies of approximately one OROV-positive individual per 10,000 vectors sampled [71, 72]. Our median estimates of the infected vector-to-human ratio (𝑉/𝐻), ranging from 1.32 to 1.52 across the three clusters, were compatible with a substantial pool of infected vectors unrepresented in the genomic dataset. The limited biological information and exclusive reliance on human-derived sequences, when combined, constrained our ability to disentangle the incubation and infectious periods in vectors, thereby limiting the temporal detail with which we could characterize vector-human transmission. The relatively broad prediction intervals for some duration-related parameters further illustrate the uncertainty associated with these estimates.

The availability of human-derived genomic data also limited the application of our estimator. Most identified genomic clusters were relatively small, and the temporal distribution of available sequences did not necessarily reflect that of reported cases in the corresponding states. Sparse genomic sampling, together with the limited phylogenetic resolution of OROV genomic data, constrained the epidemiological information recoverable from these trees. Consequently, only a subset of the identified clusters was suitable for inference using the DL estimator. This limitation was particularly consequential for the CE-2025 subcluster, which circulated in the same geographical region as CE-2024 during a subsequent outbreak. Its inclusion would have enabled a comparison of transmission dynamics across successive outbreaks within a shared regional setting. Unlike CE-2024, CE-2025 circulated during the state's rainy season and coincided with higher reported incidence, providing an opportunity to investigate temporal variation in transmissibility and its potential association with seasonal conditions. Such a comparison would reduce the geographical heterogeneity inherent in comparisons across regions, although the greater involvement of urban areas in the 2025 outbreak [73] would introduce ecological differences that would need to be considered. Although the 44 genomes in CE-2025 placed it within the range supported by our estimator, its highly polytomous phylogeny provided insufficient information for reliable inference, as assessed via its summary statistics.

Application of the DL estimator to major clusters of the 𝑀 1 𝐿 2 𝑆 2 lineage in Brazil yielded broadly comparable median estimates of total infection duration in vectors and humans across the northern (AM-I), southeastern (ES-I), and northeastern (CE-2024) regions, with overlapping 95% PIs. Median estimates ranged from 15 (AM-I) to 19 days (ES-I) in vectors and from 9 (AM-I) to 12 days (CE-2024) in humans. Although empirical data on the course of OROV infection remain limited, particularly in vectors, previous studies provide plausibility for these estimates in both host types [11, 71, 74, 75]. However, our simulation-based validation revealed a tendency to overestimate duration-related parameters, warranting caution when interpreting both their absolute values and their apparent similarity across clusters.

These broadly similar estimates are compatible with transmission involving vector populations with comparable biological characteristics and human populations with similar infection kinetics. However, neither possibility can currently be evaluated directly. Entomological studies reporting OROV-positive specimens remain scarce; despite the scale of the 2022-2025 outbreak in Brazil, no published studies have documented vector detections associated with the outbreak [72]. Shared environmental features across tropical transmission settings in northern [16], northeastern [21, 24, 73], and southeastern [20, 23] Brazil are compatible with the involvement of vector populations with similar ecological characteristics, but do not establish their taxonomic identity or relative contribution to transmission. In humans, determining whether infection kinetics differed across regions would require prospective cohort studies combining well-resolved information on exposure timing with serial sampling and assays for infectious virus to estimate incubation and infectiousness periods [75]. Such comparative data are currently unavailable.

As with infection durations, estimates of the composite reproduction number, 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 , were broadly comparable across clusters, ranging from 1.15 (ES-I) to 1.81 (CE-2024), with overlapping 95% PIs. However, because 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 = 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 , similar composite values can arise from different combinations of the directional reproduction numbers. In AM-I and ES-I, point estimates of 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 (1.45 and 1.38, respectively) exceeded those of 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 (0.73 and 0.85, respectively), whereas CE-2024 showed the reverse pattern, with 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 = 1.55 and 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 = 1.09. These estimates suggest differences in the relative contributions of the two stages of the transmission cycle. Assuming comparable vector competence, per-vector biting rates, and human infectiousness across settings, the higher 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 estimated for CE-2024 could reflect greater exposure of infectious humans to susceptible vectors. Such exposure could also contribute to a higher ratio of infected vectors to infected humans (𝑉/𝐻), a quantity distinct from the overall vector-to-human abundance ratio. Consistent with this hypothesis, the median estimated 𝑉/𝐻 was slightly higher in CE-2024 (1.52) than in AM-I (1.32) and ES-I (1.47). Nevertheless, 𝑉/𝐻 was the least reliably estimated of the six quantities in our validation analyses, and these modest differences therefore provide limited support for this hypothesis.

An additional finding from our analyses was the robustness of 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 estimation to variation in the sampling proportion, with negligible changes in estimates when the assumed number of cases associated with transmission was increased by up to 50%. This result is particularly relevant given evidence that epidemiological surveillance may fail to detect a substantial fraction of OROV infections [73, [76] [77] [78] [79]. Underascertainment may arise from the nonspecific clinical presentation of OROF, which overlaps with that of dengue and other febrile illnesses [4] in settings where multiple arboviruses circulate [21, 80], as well as from asymptomatic or oligosymptomatic infections [73]. A population-based serosurvey conducted after the outbreak in Baturité, Ceará, found that approximately 75% of seropositive participants reported no history of Oropouche fever, consistent with a substantial burden of asymptomatic, oligosymptomatic, or otherwise unrecognized infections [73].

To complement the constant 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 estimates obtained for each phylogeny and better characterize the epidemiological dynamics of individual transmission clusters, we applied a systematic temporal sub sampling approach, advancing from the root of each tree in seven-day increments to assess variation in 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 over time. For AM-I, the temporal distribution of sampled genomes closely mirrored that of reported cases, enabling estimation of 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 during rapid epidemic growth.

Estimates ranged from 4.10 (95% PI: 2.6-5.1) to 4.43 (95% PI: 2.6-5.4) in epidemiological week (EW) 51 of 2023 (17-23 December). The estimated peak in 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 preceded the peak in reported cases by approximately three weeks. This lag may reflect the continued accumulation of infections following peak transmission potential, compounded by delays associated with both incubation periods and case reporting. The subsequent peak in statewide case counts may also reflect the expansion of other transmission clusters co-circulating in Amazonas [16]. Using weekly reported case counts for Brazil, Rodriguez-Morales et al. [81] estimated 𝑅 0 at 2.87 (95% CI: 2.36-3.55) using an exponential-growth method and 3.79 (95% CI: 3.30-4.35) using a maximum-likelihood method during the early growth phase of the first epidemic wave (EW 45-50 of 2023), when approximately 70% of reported cases were concentrated in Amazonas. The substantial overlap between confidence intervals of those estimates suggests broad compatibility between the epidemiological and phylodynamic findings. Nevertheless, differences in geographical scope, temporal aggregation, number of genetic clusters considered, and parameter definition warrant caution in direct comparisons between studies.

For CE-2024, the highest 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 estimate obtained through our cumulative approach was 3.0 (95% PI: 1.5-4.5), corresponding to epidemiological week (EW) 29 of 2024 (16-22 July). This median estimate was lower than that obtained for AM-I, however, overlapped substantially. Moreover, direct comparisons warrant caution because the two clusters circulated in distinct geographical and seasonal contexts. While the spread of the AM-I clade between late 2023 and early 2024 coincided with the rainy season in Amazonas, most reported cases in Ceará in 2024 occurred during July and August, outside the state's rainy season. Regardless of its potential relative to the endemic region, these findings suggest substantial transmission potential for OROV in a non-endemic northeastern region, even outside the optimal period of rainy season.

For ES-I, the temporal distribution of genomic sampling was poorly aligned with that of reported cases, with sequences collected across periods of markedly different epidemiological activity rather than being concentrated around the epidemic peak. Consequently, although sufficient phylogenetic information for cumulative 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 inference became available during the rapid increase in reported cases, these estimates incorporated genomic information accumulated over a prolonged and epidemiologically heterogeneous period, including months of substantially lower reported incidence. This temporal heterogeneity may have obscured changes in transmission intensity during the epidemic expansion, potentially contributing to the relatively stable 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 estimates observed for ES-I. Interpretation is further complicated by the co-circulation of multiple transmission clusters in Espírito Santo [19], whose relative contributions to statewide incidence and temporal patterns of expansion remain unresolved. Using Bayesian inference based on daily case counts, Delatorre et al. [20] estimated an instantaneous reproduction number (𝑅 𝑡 ) of approximately 2.5 between epidemiological weeks (EWs) 18 and 27 of 2024, reaching a peak of approximately 3.0 in EW 26. However, this earlier period of elevated transmission was not captured by our cumulative analysis, precluding a direct comparison between the epidemiological and phylodynamic estimates during that phase of the outbreak.

Future development of the BDEIVH framework should include extending inference to larger phylogenies and broadening the simulation datasets used for training. Training on trees with more than 350 tips would enable the analysis of larger transmission clusters, including those encountered in other arboviral systems, while allowing us to assess whether the observed gains in predictive accuracy persist beyond the current size range. Increasing the number of training trees may also improve performance by providing denser coverage of parameter space. For several parameters, however, improvements were modest across the larger tree-size categories. This pattern could reflect limitations in the information conveyed by the phylogenies, the training data, or the estimator. Evaluating training dataset size and phylogeny size jointly would help distinguish these possibilities and establish whether additional simulations improve inference where larger trees offer limited gains.

A further extension would be to introduce a skyline formulation [53], allowing key parameters to vary across successive time intervals within a transmission cluster. This would enable the framework to characterize temporal variation in transmissibility that may be obscured by estimates averaged over the cluster's history. Such flexibility would be particularly relevant to arboviral outbreaks, where transmission dynamics can change with seasonality [82] [83] [84] [85], vector abundance [85] [86] [87], population susceptibility [88, 89], and control measures [90] [91] [92]. The biological basis of the model could also be strengthened as more precise estimates of vectorand host-specific parameters become available. Where OROV-specific evidence remains scarce, experimental and epidemiological studies of related arboviruses could help inform plausible ranges for the extrinsic incubation period and the infectious periods in vectors and vertebrate hosts. The applicability of these estimates would nevertheless require careful assessment, given potential differences among virus-vector-host systems and the environmental conditions under which they were obtained.

Finally, a further extension would be to integrate reported case counts with phylogenetic data within the BDEIVH framework. Particle filtering offers a way to combine these complementary sources of information by representing plausible epidemic trajectories as a collection of particles, each corresponding to a distinct realization of the underlying epidemic process in the likelihoodbased context [93] [94] [95]. In the DL context, case counts could be represented as additional features associated with input tree data. For OROV, this approach could help resolve temporal variation in 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 and better constrain infection dynamics in human and vector populations. The observation and simulation models would need to accommodate under reporting, reporting delays, and changes in surveillance practices, while ensuring that case counts correspond to the population represented by the phylogeny. Developing this extension would also require an explicit representation of the relationship between case reporting and genomic sampling.

This study advances arboviral phylodynamics by combining for the first time an explicit representation of the alternating vertebrate-vector-vertebrate transmission cycle with a DL approach that makes parameter inference computationally tractable. Applied to OROV, the estimator yielded epidemiologically plausible estimates of transmission parameters across distinct Brazilian regions. Its relevance extends beyond OROV, providing a methodological foundation for studying other arboviruses, subject to appropriate biological parameterization and validation. Future work should prioritize expanding the size and diversity of training datasets, incorporating time-varying transmission parameters, refining biological parameterization, and integrating epidemiological data into the inference framework. These developments would strengthen our ability to investigate how ecological conditions shape arboviral transmission and the resulting burden of disease.

4 Materials and Methods

4.1 The Birth-Death Exposed-Infectious Vector-Humans (BDEIVH) model

To capture the dynamics of arboviral transmission in urban cycles (Fig. 1a) and enable their subsequent integration into a DL framework, we developed the Birth-Death Exposed-Infectious Vector-Human (BDEIVH) model (Fig. 1b), a MTBD process that explicitly represents pathogen transmission between vector and human hosts. The model comprises four epidemiological states: exposed vectors (𝑉 𝐸 ), infectious vectors (𝑉 𝐼 ), exposed humans (𝐻 𝐸 ), and infectious humans (𝐻 𝐼 ). Exposed individuals are infected but not yet capable of onward transmission, whereas infectious individuals transmit infection between hosts at rates 𝜆 𝑉 𝐻 (vector-to-human) and 𝜆 𝐻𝑉 (human-to-vector). Progression from the exposed to the infectious state occurs at rates 𝜇 𝑉 and 𝜇 𝐻 , corresponding to the inverse of the mean extrinsic (vector) and intrinsic (human) incubation periods. Infectious vectors and humans are removed from the transmission process at rates 𝜓 𝑉 and 𝜓 𝐻 , representing the inverse of their mean infectious periods (for definitions and interpretations of phylodynamic parameters see [96, 97]). Human infections are sampled upon removal with probability 𝜌 𝐻 , whereas vector infections are sampled with probability 𝜌 𝑉.

The model is parameterized by two directional reproduction numbers: and where 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 denotes the expected number of human infections generated by a single infectious vector, and 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 denotes the expected number of vector infections generated by a single infectious human.

We also define 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 (Fig. 1c), a composite human-to-human reproduction number associated with a complete transmission cycle involving both humans and vectors, which is defined as: which quantifies the expected number of secondary human infections generated by a single infectious human through one complete vector-mediated transmission cycle.

4.2 Simulation Parameters

The DL-implemented BDEIVH estimator was trained using tree datasets simulated under parameters informed by OROV biology in both vector and human hosts, as well as by genomic surveillance data from Brazil (Table 1). Pinheiro et al. [71] reported an extrinsic incubation period of 6-12 days. As for the infectious period in vectors, Roberts et al. [74] observed approximately 50% mortality among field-collected vectors after 10-11 days under laboratory conditions, with mortality reaching 100% ≈ 6 days later. The age of the individuals at the time of capture was unknown, limiting the extent to which these observations can be interpreted as estimates of total adult longevity. Given the limited empirical information available to independently parameterize the incubation (𝐷 𝑉-𝐼 𝑁𝐶 ) and infectious (𝐷 𝑉-𝐼 𝑁 𝐹 ) periods, these components were jointly represented as the total duration of infection in vectors (𝐷 𝑉 ), ranging uniformly between 10 and 20 days, from which the incubation and infectious periods were randomly sampled.

The intrinsic incubation period was initially reported by Pinheiro et al. [11] to range from 4-8 days, whereas the infectious period generally lasted 2-5 days, although durations of up to 10 days were also observed. The median incubation period for OROV was estimated at 3.2 days, with the 5th and 95th percentiles of the incubation-period distribution estimated at approximately 1.1 and 9.7 days, respectively [75]. Consistent with the parameterization adopted for vectors, the incubation (𝐷 𝐻-𝐼 𝑁𝐶 ) and infectious (𝐷 𝐻-𝐼 𝑁 𝐹 ) periods in humans were jointly represented as the total duration of infection, 𝐷 𝐻 , with a uniform range of 3 to 15 days.

The vector-to-human and human-to-vector reproduction numbers, 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 and 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 , respectively, were parameterized such that their product corresponded to 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 , which was sampled uniformly between 1 and 5. This range was informed by two OROV studies in Brazil. First, a nationwide analysis of the 2023-2024 epidemic peaks estimated median 𝑅 𝑡 values ranging from 2.87 to 4.26, with the upper bounds of the corresponding 95% confidence intervals reaching 4.73 [81]. Second, an analysis conducted in the state of Espírito Santo inferred a median 𝑅 𝑡 of approximately 2.5, with peak values reaching 3.0 [20]. For each simulation, 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 was first sampled from its predefined range, after which 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 was sampled uniformly between 0.5 and 2𝑅 𝐻𝐻 . The corresponding value of 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 was then constrained by the relationship 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 = 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 /𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 . Therefore, both 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 and 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 were allowed to vary within an overall range of 0.5 to 10, while still satisfying the relation 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 = 𝑅 𝐻𝐻.

The last two parameters were informed by genomic clusters previously described in Brazil [16, 20, 21]. The sampling proportion in humans, 𝜌 𝐻 , was allowed to vary between 1% and 50%, while the vector sampling proportion, 𝜌 𝑉 , was fixed at zero since no OROV genome sequences derived from vector samples were available. Regarding tree size, four categories were considered: (i) 30-50, (ii) 50-150, (iii) 150-250, and (iv) 250-350 tips, enabling the evaluation of the effect of tree size on the predictive performance of the DL estimator.

4.3 Tree Simulation

Tree datasets were simulated using treesimulator v.0.2.3 [60], available at https://github.com/evolbioinfo/treesimulator. For each of the four tree-size categories, three independent datasets were generated: a training set comprising 𝑛 = 100,000 trees, a calibration set comprising 𝑛 = 2,000 trees, and a test set comprising 𝑛 = 1,000 trees (see Neural Network Architecture and Estimator Inference Uncertainty) (Fig. S1a-j). In addition to the parameters described above, the ratio between the numbers of vector and human hosts represented in each tree (𝑉/𝐻) was recorded. Thus, twelve quantities were retained for each simulated tree: 𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 , 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 , 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 , 𝐷 𝑉 , 𝐷 𝑉-𝐼 𝑁𝐶 , 𝐷 𝑉-𝐼 𝑁 𝐹 , 𝐷 𝐻 , 𝐷 𝐻-𝐼 𝑁𝐶 , 𝐷 𝐻-𝐼 𝑁 𝐹 , 𝑉/𝐻, 𝜌 𝐻 , and the number of tips.

4.4 Generation of OROV-like Datasets

To generate phylogenies that more closely resemble those observed empirically, we applied a transformation procedure analogous to that described by Xie et al. [70] to training, test, and calibration tree sets, with modifications tailored to OROV. Briefly, idealized time-scaled fully bifurcated trees were transformed into OROV-like phylogenies by assigning a number of nucleotide substitutions to each branch according to a Poisson process parameterized by (i) the branch duration in years, (ii) the estimated OROV evolutionary rate (1.2 × 10 -3 , 𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑠/𝑠𝑖𝑡𝑒/𝑦𝑒𝑎𝑟 SD = 7.5 × 10 -5 ) [16], and (iii) the complete genome length of the three segments (L, M, and S) concatenated (11, 874 nucleotides) [3]. Branches assigned less than one substitution were subsequently collapsed, reproducing the loss of phylogenetic resolution that occurs when closely related viral genomes are genetically indistinguishable. In contrast to the original procedure [70], the resulting polytomies were retained rather than arbitrarily resolved, thereby avoiding the introduction of branching relationships unsupported by the simulated genetic data. The transformed trees were subsequently re-dated using LSD2 v2.4.4 [98] to generate time-scaled OROV-like phylogenies that were then used to train the DL estimator.

4.5 Phylogenetic Tree Encoding

The simulated trees were encoded following the principles introduced by PhyloCNN [68], using a windowing approach in which the local neighborhood of each internal node and leaf is represented by a set of tree-derived features. Given the comparable performance obtained when encoding two or three hierarchical levels of node neighborhoods, we restricted the representation to two levels (No-context and 1-neighborhood), thereby reducing the dimensionality of the encoded data [68]. Accordingly, 10 features were retained from the original PhyloCNN encoding.

From the No-context level: (i) sampling probability of the tree (informed alongside the supplied empirical trees); (ii) time from the focal node to the root; (iii) time from the focal node to the present; (iv) time from the focal node to its parent; and (v) number of descendant leaves. From the 1-neighborhood level: (vi) time from the focal node to its grandparent; (vii) time to the child with the smaller number of descendant leaves; (viii) time to the child with the larger number of descendant leaves; (ix) number of leaves descending from the child with the smaller number of descendant leaves; (x) number of leaves descending from the child with the larger number of descendant leaves. When polytomies were present, either in the OROV-like trees or in the empirical tree, they were retained. To explicitly incorporate information on polytomies into the tree representation, two additional features were recorded for each focal node: (xi) the median number of descendant leaves subtended by each of its direct children; and (xii) the standard deviation of the number of descendant leaves subtended by each of its direct children.

4.6 Neural Network Architecture

The DL estimator was adapted from PhyloCNN [68] and implemented in Python using TensorFlow v.2.13.0 [99] and Keras v.2.13.1 [100]. Each encoded phylogeny was represented as two separate input channels, corresponding to leaves and internal nodes. Within each channel, leaves and internal nodes were independently ordered according to their distance (in terms of number of generations) from the root and zero-padded to a maximum of 350 rows, resulting in an input tensor of dimensions 350 × 12 × 2, where the 12 features correspond to the tree-derived attributes (see Tree Encoding) and the two channels distinguish leaves from internal nodes. The convolutional component followed a depthwise separable architecture. First, a depthwise convolutional layer with 32 filters and a 1 × 12 kernel was applied using two groups, such that the leaf and internal-node channels were processed separately. This was followed by a pointwise convolutional layer comprising 32 1 × 1 filters, which combined information across the two channels, and by an additional nonlinear convolutional layer with 32 1 × 1 filters. Each convolutional layer used an exponential linear unit (ELU) activation function and was followed by batch normalization. The resulting 32 feature maps were subsequently summarized by global average pooling and passed to a feed-forward neural network comprising four fully connected layers with 64, 32, 16, and 8 neurons, respectively, each using ELU activation. Finally, the output head generated 18 (3 × 6) intermediate values, corresponding to three outputs for each of the six epidemiological parameters targeted for inference (𝑅 𝑉 𝐻 , 𝑅 𝐻𝑉 , 𝑅 𝐻𝐻 , 𝐷 𝑉 , 𝐷 𝐻 , and 𝑉/𝐻). These outputs were transformed into the 2.5%, 50%, and 97.5% conditional quantiles (see Estimator Inference Uncertainty).

4.7 Estimator Inference Uncertainty

The network was trained using the pinball loss [101], allowing the estimation of the 2.5%, 50%, and 97.5% conditional quantiles for each epidemiological parameter. The pinball loss function for a quantile 𝜏 was defined as: where 𝑒 = 𝑦 -ŷ𝜏 and 𝜏 ∈ {0.025, 0.5, 0.975}.

The predicted quantiles were made positive and structurally dependent rather than treated as unconstrained independent outputs. Given three raw network outputs, 𝑧 1 , 𝑧 2 , and 𝑧 3 , the lower, median, and upper quantiles were defined as: 𝑄0.5 = 𝑄 0.025 + softplus(𝑧 2 ), (6) and 𝑄0.975 = 𝑄 0.5 + softplus(𝑧 3 ), thereby guaranteeing0 ≤ 𝑄0.025 ≤ 𝑄0.5 ≤ 𝑄 0.975 and preventing quantile crossing.

Finally, the resulting prediction intervals were calibrated using conformalized quantile regression (CQR) [102] on an independent calibration dataset. For each calibration observation, the conformity score was calculated as: and the corresponding conformal correction, q, was subsequently used to obtain the calibrated prediction interval: thereby improving the empirical coverage of the estimated uncertainty intervals.

4.8 Estimator Predictive Performance

To evaluate the performance of the DL estimator, we compared its parameter predictions with the corresponding true values in independent test datasets (n = 1,000 per tree-size category) comprising trees sampled from the same size ranges and represented using the same encoding procedures as those used for training. Estimator performance was quantified using the mean relative bias (MRB) and mean relative error (MRE), as proposed by Voznica et al. [56]: and where 𝑛 denotes the number of trees in the test dataset, 𝜃 𝑖 is the true value of a given epidemiological parameter used to simulate the 𝑖th tree, and θ𝑖 is the corresponding estimate produced by the estimator.

4.9 Genomic Dataset and Genotyping

To identify major genomic clusters within the OROV 𝑀 1 𝐿 2 𝑆 2 lineage in Brazil, all publicly available genomes (n = 980) meeting the following criteria were downloaded from the GISAID EpiArbo platform (https://gisaid.org/): (i) complete (L, M, and S segments); (ii) highquality (≤ 5% unidentified positions); (iii) collected in the country between 2015, when the earliest sequence assigned to this lineage was sampled [103], and 2025; (iv) accompanied by complete sampling dates (day, month, and year); and (v) sampling location specified at state level. All segments were genotyped following the methodology and nomenclature proposed by Naveca et al. [16]. Datasets were aligned using MAFFT v7.526 [104], and the resulting alignments were manually curated using Aliview v1.32 [105] when necessary. Maximum-likelihood (ML) phylogenetic trees were inferred independently for the L, M, and S segments using IQ-TREE v3.1.3 [106]. The best-fitting nucleotide substitution model for each segment was selected using ModelFinder [107], yielding TIM3+F+I+G4 for the L and M segments and K3Pu+F+I+G4 for the S segment. Branch support was assessed using the Shimodaira-Hasegawa-like approximate likelihood-ratio test (SH-aLRT) with 1,000 replicates [108]. Genotypes were defined based on phylogenetic clustering with significant branch support (SH-aLRT values ≥ 0.9).

4.10 Spatiotemporal Dynamics

All genomes sampled in Brazil during the study period (n = 980) were classified as belonging to the 𝑀 1 𝐿 2 𝑆 2 lineage. Their genome segments were concatenated into a single alignment comprising 11,874 nucleotide positions, from which a maximum-likelihood (ML) phylogenetic tree was inferred using the TIM3+F+I+G4 nucleotide substitution model selected by ModelFinder [107], following the previously described inference procedure. The temporal signal of the resulting ML phylogeny was assessed through a root-to-tip regression analysis using TempEst v1.5.3 [109].

Sequences with residuals outside 𝑄 1 -1.5 × IQR and 𝑄 3 + 1.5 × IQR were considered outliers and excluded, as they are likely the result of incorrect date assignment or sequencing errors. Following removal of temporal outliers, a new ML phylogeny was constructed with the final dataset (n = 913) and time-scaled using LSD2 v2.4.4 [98]. Ancestral geographic states were reconstructed across the tree nodes using PastML v.1.9.51 [110] under the F81 model of character evolution and the marginal posterior probabilities approximation (MPPA) method. Sequences were assigned discrete geographic states according to their state of sampling in Brazil.

4.11 Genomic Cluster Selection

To be retained for phylodynamic analyses, genomic clusters were required to meet the following criteria: (i) strong statistical support (SH-aLRT ≥ 0.80); (ii) between 30 and 350 genomes, matching the range of tree sizes used to train the DL estimator; (iii) reconstruction of the ancestral node with high confidence (marginal probability ≥ 0.90); and (iv) concordance between the inferred ancestral state and the sampling location of sequences within the cluster, with ≥ 95% of sequences sampled from the same state, after excluding those from other locations that formed supported clusters (SH-aLRT ≥ 0.90). Additionally, to ensure congruence between the OROV-like training tree set and the selected empirical clusters, both were evaluated using phylogenetic summary statistics following Saulnier et al. [111]. The clusters for which more than one statistic deviated by more than three standard deviations from the corresponding training set were excluded from subsequent analyses.

For each retained genomic cluster, the number of associated cases was estimated by scaling the total number of reported cases according to the proportion of genomes assigned to the cluster: where 𝐺 𝑐 is the number of genomes in cluster 𝑐, and 𝐺 𝐼 and 𝐶 𝐼 are, respectively, the total numbers of genomes and reported cases from the corresponding location during the interval between the cluster 𝑡 MRCA and its most recently sampled sequence.

The genomic sampling probability was then calculated as: where 𝑝 𝑐 represents the proportion of estimated cases represented by sampled genomes.

4.12 Statistical Analysis

To evaluate whether inference accuracy improved with increasing tree size, relative errors were compared across the four ordered tree-size categories using the one-sided Jonckheere-Terpstra test [112, 113], with the alternative hypothesis specifying a decreasing trend in relative error as tree size increased. Pairwise differences in relative error among tree-size categories were further assessed using Dunn's test [114], with 𝑃-values adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Holm method [115]. Potential systematic bias in parameter estimation was evaluated independently within each tree-size category using two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [116], with the null hypothesis that the mean relative bias was equal to zero. For each parameter, 𝑃-values obtained across the four tree-size categories were adjusted for multiple testing using the Holm method [115].

4.13 Epidemiological and Spatial Data

Epidemiological data on the number of OROV infections in Brazil between 2023 and 2025 were obtained from the Ministry of Health (https://www.gov.br/saude/pt-br/assuntos/saude-de-a-a-z/o/oropouche/painel-epidemiologico). The boundaries of Brazilian states were obtained from the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (https://www.ibge.gov.br/en/), using the geobr R package [117].

4.14 Data Availability

The Oropouche virus (OROV) genome sequences and associated metadata used in this study were retrieved from the GISAID EpiArbo database (https://gisaid.org/), being accessible through the EPI_SET_261117qg identifier (https://doi.org/10.55876/gis8.261117qg). Statistical visualizations were generated in R using ggplot2 v.4.0.3 [118], whereas phylogenetic trees were visualized using ggtree v.4.2.0 [119]. Phylogenetic tree parsing and manipulation were performed using ETE3 v.3.1.3 [120]. The Snakemake [121] pipelines, source code for training, test and calibration dataset generation, and tree encoding, as well as Jupyter notebooks used for estimator training and testing, and source code for epidemiological parameter inference with DL-and maximum-likelihood-based estimators are available on GitHub at https://github.com/modpath/bdeivh. The repository also contains the newick files with genomic clusters analyzed in this study, as well as the pretrained BDEIVH DL models. The BDEIVH estimators are also available as a command-line program and a Python 3 package via PyPi (bdeivh), and via Docker/Singularity (evolbioinfo/bdeivh).
